title: Will the UN vote to sustain Haiti’s Gang Suppression Force?
gist: Ahead of the UN Security Council's 30 September 2026 vote on renewing Haiti's Gang Suppression Force, Chatham House argues the security mandate must be renewed but is insufficient: with USAID eliminated and the US lacking the standing to convene donors, the next phase depends on the US DFC, multilateral banks and a broad donor coalition using benchmark-conditional financing rather than conventional concessional loans to an interim government too broken to take on debt. New Chatham House-QQ survey data (May 2026) shows only 49.5 per cent of voting-age Haitians approve of the GSF and 54.2 per cent doubt it can accomplish its mission, framing a narrow and closing window.

themes.theme: GSF renewal timing and mandate risk

insights.claim: The UN Security Council votes on 30 September 2026 on renewing Haiti's Gang Suppression Force, a multinational security mission whose lapse would remove the only external force backstopping the Haitian National Police against gangs controlling almost all of Port-au-Prince.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A hard, dated catalyst for Caribbean security risk, regional migration flows and any Haiti-exposed insurance, shipping or aid budgeting — watch the 30 September resolution text for mandate length and funding language.
insights.quote: On 30 September the UN Security Council will vote on renewing the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) for Haiti.
insights.locator: On 30 September the UN Security Council

insights.claim: The window to convert Haitians' currently modest optimism about improved security into durable gains may close quickly, meaning delay or a weakened mandate at the renewal vote would forfeit the fragile progress made since the first GSF contingent arrived.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Time-decay on stabilization means the difference between a clean renewal and a contested one is likely non-linear — a stalled vote should be read as materially raising the probability of state collapse, not as a delay.
insights.quote: But the window of opportunity to channel even this limited support may close quickly.
insights.locator: At best, Haitians are modestly optimistic

insights.claim: The 2025 Security Council resolution creating the GSF was a rare UN success that passed only after earlier Haiti resolutions had been vetoed by China and Russia, making the 2026 renewal a live test of whether that coalition still holds.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Renewal is not procedural — veto-wielders have blocked Haiti action before, so pricing in automatic rollover of the mandate underestimates the geopolitical tail risk.
insights.quote: The GSF resolution of 2025 was a rare victory for the UN after past resolutions had been vetoed by China and Russia.
insights.locator: Much is at stake for the United Nations

insights.claim: The GSF is presented as a replicable template for semi-ad hoc coalitions — including Global South troop and in-kind contributors — responding to humanitarian crises without a full UN peacekeeping architecture, with Kenya and Chad supplying troops, Canada, Germany, Qatar and the US supplying funding, and Mexico, Colombia, El Salvador, Jamaica and Brazil supplying training, materiel and advisors.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: If this burden-sharing model survives renewal, expect it to be copied for future crises — a structural shift away from US- or UN-led intervention toward coalition-of-the-willing security provision with Global South manpower.
insights.quote: The Haiti resolution demonstrates that the international community can come together, even in this semi-ad hoc fashion, to respond to humanitarian crises – even when faith in the international system is waning.
insights.locator: Kenya and Chad contributed troops

insights.claim: Haiti has held no election since 2016 and currently has no elected government at any level — local, departmental, parliamentary or presidential — so the diplomatic mantra that solutions must be 'Haitian-led' has no institutional counterparty to lead.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Any policy, loan or reform program predicated on a legitimate Haitian government signing and enforcing it is built on a counterparty that does not exist — a critical flaw to check in donor and development-bank proposals.
insights.quote: Haiti hasn’t had an election since 2016. There is no elected government at any level – local, departmental, parliamentary or presidential.
insights.locator: But how are Haitians supposed to lead?

insights.claim: More than 75 per cent of Haitians do not trust their political leadership, and political parties remain in disarray under the same distrusted leaders who have dominated for decades, per a Chatham House-QQ survey.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Legitimacy deficits of this magnitude mean elections alone would not produce a credible partner; assume a long horizon before any Haitian administration can be treated as a reliable sovereign counterparty.
insights.quote: more than 75 per cent of Haitians don’t trust their political leadership
insights.locator: Indeed, according to a Chatham House-QQ survey

insights.claim: Years of international development support have failed to produce a Haitian civil society capable of substituting for government, leaving it fragmented, weak and distant from political power — an implicit verdict that the prior aid model did not work.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Donors repeating the civil-society-capacity-building playbook should be treated sceptically; the article implies vehicles with investment and results discipline will outperform grant-based institution building.
insights.quote: And civil society remains fragmented, weak and often distant from political power – despite years of international development support.
insights.locator: And civil society remains fragmented

insights.claim: Because Haitians cannot realistically lead their own recovery in the absence of elected institutions, responsibility for stabilizing the country falls back onto the international community — a conclusion that cuts directly against the prevailing post-2021 diplomatic consensus.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect rhetoric about local ownership to be quietly displaced by more interventionist, conditionality-heavy external programs — a signal for where donor money and political capital will actually flow.
insights.quote: It’s a nice phrase, intended to reassure sceptics that a solution would not be imposed on Haiti.
insights.locator: ‘Haitian-led’

themes.theme: Survey evidence: split and sceptical public support

insights.claim: Approximately 1,300 gang leaders and members were killed in Haitian National Police operations in the period leading up to May 2026, aided by the arrival of the first 400 Chadian GSF troops in April 2026 and by fractures within the gang coalition controlling parts of Haiti's economy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Gang-coalition fragmentation, not just external force, drove the recent gains — meaning security progress is reversible if the gangs re-consolidate, and the improvement is a weaker signal than the casualty count implies.
insights.quote: An estimated 1,300 gang leaders and members were killed in those operations.
insights.locator: Fragile progress

insights.claim: Only 49.5 per cent of voting-age Haitians approved or strongly approved of the GSF multinational force in May 2026, and 54.2 per cent do not believe it can accomplish its mission — a majority-sceptical public even during a period of improving security.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Below-majority approval and majority doubt cap how much political cover the force has locally; a single high-casualty incident could flip public opinion and undermine the renewal's durability.
insights.quote: Yet 54.2 per cent of Haitians polled don’t believe the GSF can accomplish its mission.
insights.locator: But support for the GSF was mixed

insights.claim: GSF support is strongest exactly where insecurity is worst and among the young: over 67 per cent approval among Haitians in or near gang-controlled areas, and 58.4 per cent among 18-29 year olds, versus 49.5 per cent nationally.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Proximity to violence, not ideology, drives support — the constituency that matters most for recovery (under-30s) backs intervention, a positive indicator for sustaining the mission if it can show results.
insights.quote: 58.4 per cent of Haitians between the ages of 18 and 29 – a key demographic for Haiti’s recovery and future – also showed strong support for the GSF.
insights.locator: Unsurprisingly, that support was greater

insights.claim: A slight majority of Haitians (50.7 per cent) believed by May 2026 that their communities had become safer, marking the first measurable turn in perceived security since the post-2021 collapse.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A bare majority is the thinnest possible mandate; track whether this figure rises in subsequent surveys as the leading indicator of whether the GSF model is actually working.
insights.quote: a slight majority of Haitians (50.7 per cent) were starting to believe that their communities had become safer
insights.locator: At the time of the survey

insights.claim: Haitians themselves rank education (69.1 per cent) and healthcare (67.3 per cent) as the top priorities for re-establishing security — higher than their approval of the security force itself — implying the population sees service delivery, not kinetic operations, as the route to stability.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A security-only mandate renewal without parallel service funding will likely fail to convert into public legitimacy; watch whether the Security Council discussion extends beyond security language.
insights.quote: Respondents to the Chatham House-QQ survey identified education and healthcare as priorities in re-establishing security: 69.1 per cent and 67.3 per cent respectively.
insights.locator: Respondents to the Chatham House-QQ survey identified

insights.claim: With USAID eliminated, no institution is currently positioned to coordinate Haiti's development recovery, and the United States is judged to lack the resources, commitment and moral authority to convene a donors' conference — a blunt assessment of degraded US convening power.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The collapse of US-led aid coordination is a structural change, not a Haiti anecdote — expect coordination gaps, slower disbursement and a scramble for substitute conveners across every fragile-state theatre.
insights.quote: The US now lacks the resources, commitment and moral authority to convene a donors’ conference and mobilize resources and commitments for Haitians’ needs.
insights.locator: Without the US Agency for International Development

insights.claim: Conventional concessional lending from development banks is unworkable in Haiti because the interim government is too broken to take on sovereign debt, so banks should instead build incentive-based, conditional partnerships that release funds only when benchmarks in security, fiscal, healthcare, education and macroeconomic reform are met.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A concrete template for fragile-state finance: tranche-released, benchmark-conditional grants replacing sovereign loans — relevant to how MDB portfolios and donor instruments get restructured for non-creditworthy states.
insights.quote: Haiti’s interim government is too broken to commit to such debts.
insights.locator: It will also require more than the kind of concessional loans

insights.claim: The US Development Finance Corporation is described as well-bank-rolled and capable of providing investor insurance and concessionary loans to crowd private capital into Haiti, and is argued to be likely to outperform the defunct USAID because of its focus on investment, trade and results.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A think-tank endorsement of blended finance over grant aid — watch DFC deal flow and political risk insurance capacity as the new channel through which frontier-market exposure to fragile states gets underwritten.
insights.quote: Frankly, they will probably do it better than USAID because of their focus on investment, trade and results.
insights.locator: The US Development Finance Corporation (DFC) must also play a key role

insights.claim: The DFC's mandate to 'mobilize private capital to advance US foreign policy' is proposed as a portable model that other government development agencies, private foundations and multilateral development banks should adopt, generalizing the private-capital-mobilization approach beyond the US.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals institutional convergence on DFI-style blended finance as the successor to bilateral aid — a durable demand driver for political risk insurance, guarantees and frontier private credit.
insights.quote: The DFC’s mandate to ‘mobilize private capital to advance US foreign policy’ can equally apply to other donors, including government development agencies, private foundations and multilateral development banks.
insights.locator: However, that will require a more concentrated effort by the DFC

insights.claim: The international donor community is characterized as fractured, making mobilization of development assistance for Haiti an open question that the Security Council vote is unlikely to resolve on its own.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Funding fragmentation, not political will at the UN, is the binding constraint — the real signal to watch after 30 September is whether any donors' conference is actually convened and by whom.
insights.quote: How can development assistance be mobilized for Haiti, among a fractured international donor community?
insights.locator: Now is not the time to pull the plug

insights.claim: Haiti has already become a vector for gun smuggling, narcotics trafficking and other illicit activity, and further state collapse would push it toward becoming a stateless hub for transnational crime affecting every country with an Atlantic coast — not just the Caribbean, Mexico and the US.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frames Haiti as a systemic, not localized, security risk — an argument European and Commonwealth governments will face pressure to fund, and a driver of maritime security, interdiction and border-enforcement spending far from the Caribbean.
insights.quote: The longer the crisis goes on the greater the risk that Haiti becomes a stateless hub for transnational crime – affecting every country with an Atlantic coast.
insights.locator: Rebuilding Haiti and protecting the security of Haitians

insights.claim: Rebuilding Haiti is explicitly reframed as more than a US foreign policy interest, with UK Commonwealth countries in the Caribbean named among those exposed — an argument aimed at broadening the funding base beyond Washington.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for UK, EU and Commonwealth commitments to fill the post-USAID gap; burden-shifting rhetoric usually precedes actual budget reallocation requests.
insights.quote: Rebuilding Haiti and protecting the security of Haitians by battling gangs is not just a US foreign policy interest.
insights.locator: Rebuilding Haiti and protecting the security of Haitians

insights.claim: The US approach of sequencing security and 'gang suppression' first is judged to have been necessary and successful, but is now argued to be inadequate unless development work runs in parallel rather than sequentially.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The security-first-then-development sequence is being challenged in favour of parallel tracks; a renewal that funds only security should be read as an incomplete fix with a high relapse probability.
insights.quote: There is now a need to work in parallel on social and economic development and the rebuilding of Haiti’s battered physical and institutional infrastructure.
insights.locator: The US’s commitment to focus on security
